## The Brotherhoods Against Silence: The Struggle for Generational Renewal

In the parish office of the church of the Encarnación, the leaders of the Hermandad del Cristo del Mar keep a laminated poster advertising a manual bell-ringing workshop. The date is from last autumn, and the number of registrations did not even fill half of the available spots. This scene accurately summarizes the state of a battle that the brotherhoods of Almuñécar have been waging for years against the progressive silence of their bell towers.

The Cofradía de Nuestra Señora de la Antigua, linked to the church that dominates the old town, attempted a similar strategy during the spring. They organized two introductory sessions on manual bell ringing, with the selfless collaboration of a retired bell ringer who offered to pass on the rudiments of the craft. Four people attended, two of them direct relatives of the bell ringer himself, and none returned for the second call. The heads of the brotherhoods consulted agree that the problem is not the promotion of the activity, but the nature of the commitment it requires.

The contrast with other towns in the Andalusian region is especially painful for those familiar with the bell-ringing tradition. In Villavante, a small town in León, bell ringers keep the manual tradition alive as an inheritance passed down from parents to children without the need for manuals or formal calls. There, generational renewal happens organically, because bell ringing remains integrated into daily life and the celebrations that structure the community calendar. In Almuñécar, that chain of transmission has broken at some point over the last three decades.

Young people in Almuñécar show a genuine interest in local heritage, as demonstrated by their participation in historical tours or initiatives to recover the municipality's photographic memory. However, this enthusiasm does not translate into a willingness to regularly climb the bell tower, learn the coded ringing patterns, and take on the responsibility of keeping them alive. The craft demands an availability that clashes with the work and leisure rhythms of the new generations, but also with a perception of the bell ringer as a figure from the past, detached from the concerns of the present.

Funding constitutes another structural obstacle that the brotherhoods have been unable to overcome. The budgets of these brotherhoods are primarily allocated to the conservation of images, processional floats, and liturgical items, leaving minimal margin for training activities. A manual bell-ringing workshop requires, under optimal conditions, fair remuneration for the instructor, teaching materials, and civil liability insurance covering access to the bell tower. None of the brotherhoods consulted currently have sufficient funds to sustain a continuous learning program.

The paradox is evident to those observing the situation from the outside. The bells of Almuñécar continue to ring, but they do so increasingly through electronic mechanisms that play recordings or activate automatic hammers. The sound remains, but the language disappears, because manual ringing precisely implies the ability to modulate, improvise, and adapt each toll to the specific circumstance. An automatic peal does not distinguish between a wedding and a funeral, between the patron saint festival and a weather alert.

The brotherhoods' attempts to reverse this trend have also included seeking alliances with educational centers. The Hermandad del Cristo del Mar proposed an extracurricular activity to the local secondary school that combined the history of manual bell ringing with a practical demonstration in the bell tower. The response from the teaching staff was courteous but evasive, and the initiative was shelved waiting for a schedule availability that never materialized. The episode illustrates the difficulty of integrating traditional knowledge into the margins of an educational system focused on other priorities.

Meanwhile, the veteran bell ringers who still retain the knowledge of the traditional ringing patterns are aging without a replacement. Some have begun recording home videos with their mobile phones, aware that these images may become the only available testimony for future generations. The brotherhoods keep these recordings with a zeal that reveals an awareness of preserving a heritage in a critical state, but they know that no video can replace direct transmission, the embodied learning that is only acquired by climbing the bell tower time and time again.

The struggle for generational renewal is being fought on a terrain where willpower is not enough. The brotherhoods of Almuñécar have identified the problem, designed responses, and collided with the limits of their own resources. The silence threatening the bell towers of Almuñécar is not the product of neglect, but of a combination of structural factors that no single brotherhood can solve on its own. The question left hanging in the air is whether the UNESCO declaration as Intangible Cultural Heritage will serve to mobilize the institutional support that has so far failed to materialize.
